source_text: Sed quantum interest inter plenum et vacuum, tantum nimirum inter possibilitatem et necessitatem. Possibilitas enim rei illius, cuius capax dicitur, vacua ostenditur; quando si vacua non esset, nec capax esset. Quis enim caperet, quod iam haberet? Necessitas autem non vacuitatem, sed plenitudinem indicat; non potest quippe capere quasi vacua, quod iam quasi plena esse compellit. Tantum itaque inter necessaria et possibilia interest, quantum inter conferta et inania. Ab utriusque ergo qualitatis, cuius aeque capax est, praeiudiciis ipsa repugnantium susceptione defenditur. Habet ergo bonum necessarium in natura tantum, quantum ad honorem spectat auctoris; quod est innocentia nulli malo admixta naturaliter, proprii operis pro boni proprietate et accusatione mali receptrix. Illud ergo quod ei de proprio venit, peccans quisque sauciare potest; hoc vero quod de Dei opere suscepit, decolorare non potest. Manet ergo et in malis hominibus taxatio naturalis boni; nec umquam malum erit, bonum malumque agere potuisse; sed personae illi nihil proderit, quae necessarii sui instituta non damnat quidem, sed tamen sibi ea non prodesse compulit. Sicut ergo in eo homine, in quo est iam explicata libertas, cum peccat, malum adscribimus voluntati, naturam autem Deo conditionis auctori; ita si parvulus, qui voluntatis usum non habet, nec quidquam ostendit praeter instituta naturae, scelere plenus esse dicatur, atque habere malum a necessario, quod alter a possibili capit; sine dubio is auctor criminis, qui naturae auctor, arguitur.
pass_a_gloss: But as much as there is a difference between full and empty, so much indeed between possibility and necessity. For the possibility of that thing of which it is said capable is shown empty; since if it were not empty, it would not even be capable. For who would take what he already had? But necessity indicates not emptiness, but fullness; for it cannot take as empty what it already compels to be as full. So much therefore there is a difference between necessary things and possible, as between packed and empty. From the prior judgments therefore of each quality, of which it is equally capable, it is defended by the very taking-up of things fighting. It has therefore a necessary good in nature only as much as looks to the honor of the author; which is an innocence mixed with no evil naturally, a receiver of its own work according to the property of good and the accusation of evil. That therefore which comes to it from its own, each one sinning can wound; but this which he received from God's work he cannot discolor. There remains therefore even in evil humans an assessment of natural good; nor will it ever be evil to have been able to do good and evil; but it will profit that person nothing, who indeed does not condemn the institutions of his necessary, but nevertheless compelled them not to profit himself. As therefore in that human in whom freedom is already explained, when he sins, we ascribe evil to will, but nature to God the author of the condition; so if a little one, who does not have the use of will, nor shows anything besides the institutions of nature, is said to be full of wickedness, and to have an evil from the necessary, which another takes from the possible; without doubt he is accused as the author of the charge, who is the author of nature.

pass_b_english: The difference between possibility and necessity is as great as that between fullness and emptiness. A capacity is shown empty of the thing it can receive; if it were not empty, it could not receive it. Who would receive what he already had? Necessity, however, indicates not emptiness but fullness. It cannot receive as though empty what it already compels to exist as though full. Necessary things differ from possible things, therefore, as packed things from empty things. The capacity is protected from predetermination toward either quality, for which it is equally capable, precisely by receiving opposites. It possesses in nature the necessary good that reflects its maker’s honor: innocence naturally mixed with no evil, receptive of its own acts, both the distinct merit of good and the blame of evil.

A sinner can wound what comes to him from his own activity; he cannot discolor what he received from God’s work. The valuation of natural goodness therefore remains even in evil people. It will never be evil to have been capable of doing good and evil. But it will not benefit the person who, without actually condemning the institutions of his necessary nature, has compelled them to be of no benefit to himself. In a human being whose freedom is already developed, therefore, when he sins we assign evil to will, but nature to God its creator. If, however, an infant who has no exercise of will and displays nothing except nature’s institutions is said to be full of crime, possessing by necessity the evil another receives by possibility, the one accused as crime’s author is undoubtedly nature’s author.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
